stimulus.text: When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty; because apprehensions may arise, lest the same monarch or senate should enact tyrannical laws, to execute them in a tyrannical manner. Again, there is no liberty, if the judiciary power be not separated from the legislative and executive. There would be an end of everything, were the same man or the same body, whether of the nobles or of the people, to exercise those three powers.
stimulus.source_note: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748), abridged. Public domain.

books.section: A. Protestant Evangelicalism and Enlightenment Philosophy

primary_sources: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748)

stem: Why, according to Montesquieu, is there no liberty when the same body both makes the laws and executes them?

options.text: Because the laws would be written in language ordinary people cannot read
options.misconception: Montesquieu's worry is not about the wording of laws — it is about who holds the power to make and enforce them.

options.text: Because the body would be too busy to enforce the laws fairly
options.misconception: Being busy is not Montesquieu's concern. His concern is that unchecked power turns tyrannical.

options.text: Because the judges would have no cases left to decide
options.misconception: Montesquieu does not argue about the judges' workload — he argues about liberty disappearing.

options.text: Because the same body could enact tyrannical laws and then execute them tyrannically

rationales.D: Montesquieu's fear is self-enforcement: the body that writes tyrannical laws would also carry them out, with no check. A power that polices itself is not policed at all.
rationales.A: The language of the laws is beside the point. Montesquieu fears the union of lawmaking and law-enforcing power.
rationales.B: Montesquieu never mentions overwork. His fear is tyranny, not a crowded calendar.
rationales.C: The judges' caseload is not at stake. What is at stake is liberty, which dies when powers unite.
rationales.general:
1. Follow Montesquieu's because. United powers raise the fear that the same body will enact tyrannical laws.
2. Follow it to the end. That same body would then execute those laws in a tyrannical manner.
3. Name the danger. Power that checks itself is no check at all — the lawmaker becomes its own enforcer.
Remember: a check only works when it comes from outside — a body policing itself is not policed.
